summary:
Our idea was to create three interactive maps using ESA resources that were available online.
The first is, of course, a map of Earth. By selecting the criteria of your choice (environment, temperature, etc.), this map shows you the exact location that best matches your search. 
Next is a map of the Moon. By selecting a location (such as a potential landing site for Artemis III, for example), you can choose that spot and get information about it, as well as find out which location on Earth is best suited to simulate conditions similar to those that will actually be encountered on the ground.
Finally, there’s a map of Mars with the same features. 
The source of this information is reliable; the data was collected by the ESA in its open-source document titled “The-Catalogue-of-Planetary-Analogues"
details:
Our project consists of a website featuring three interactive maps created using open data from the ESA. The first is a map of Earth: you select the characteristics that interest you (environment, temperature, etc.), and it shows you the location that best matches your criteria. The second is a map of the Moon. You select a location—for example, a potential landing site for Artemis III—and you get information about it, as well as the places on Earth that most closely resemble the conditions astronauts would face there. The third map does the same for Mars.

We wanted to make ESA’s data easier to use. The document is nearly 170 pages long, and a potential reader might feel discouraged or overwhelmed by such a large amount of information.

Finding sites usually involves sifting through a lot of data, whereas here, it only takes a few clicks. We hope this will simplify and reduce the cost of planning training and testing on Earth for lunar and Martian missions.

We developed it using several tools at our disposal, such as “Pornkbun,” which provided us with a free domain name. Claude Code helped us with the programming; the Three.js library was used for the 3D planets, and d3 and TopoJSON were used for the map. We used *The Catalogue of Planetary Analogues* because it is publicly available and well-documented.

What we consider creative is our approach: instead of following the usual path, the user has the option to start from the Moon or Mars to find a location on Earth. During the project, we had to determine which criteria would be most relevant to the user’s choices and how to ensure a high-quality website with an intuitive interface. One of the biggest challenges was making the coordinate system work on the Moon and Mars using simple 3D models and linking them to the database.
